title: Who are “the spirits in prison”, and when, where and what did he preach (1 Peter 3:19–20)?
summary: 1 Peter 3:19 says that “he went and preached unto the spirits in prison”, and 3:20 says they “sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah”. The verses do not say who “he” is in the act of going, what the prison is or where, when the going took place, or what the preaching was.
text: KJV 1 Peter 3:19: “By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) 1 Peter 3:19: ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασιν πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξεν [in which also, having gone, he proclaimed to the spirits in prison]; the Textus Receptus text served prints the same words. KJV 1 Peter 3:20: “Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah”. KJV 1 Peter 3:18: “being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/60/3/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/60/3/.
reasoning: The verse gives an act (“went and preached”) and its hearers (“the spirits in prison”), and the next verse says of them that they were disobedient in the days of Noah. It does not say what “in which” (“By which”) points back to, whether the spirits are the persons who lived in Noah’s day, or other beings, when the going and preaching happened, or whether the preaching offered anything or announced something already done. The Greek printed is ἐκήρυξεν (proclaimed, preached) and the verse does not give the content. Readings that have been held include that the preaching was done by Christ through the Spirit in Noah’s day, that it was done between his death and his rising, and that the spirits are fallen angels and not human persons. The verses quoted state none of these and the record does not choose among them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to 1 Peter 3:18–20. A word search of the packaged KJV finds the phrase “spirits in prison” only at 1 Peter 3:19. The record does not say which reading is right and does not claim that no other passage of the Bible says more. The Greek quoted is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life, checked against the Textus Receptus text served there. The Greek New Testament wording is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life (TISCH), compared with the Textus Receptus text served there (TR); neither is a critical apparatus.

title: Who are “them that are dead” to whom the gospel “was preached” (1 Peter 4:6)?
summary: 1 Peter 4:6 says “the gospel [was] preached also to them that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit”. The verse does not say whether “the dead” were dead when the gospel was preached to them or when the verse is written, or what “judged according to men in the flesh” and “live according to God in the spirit” stand for.
text: KJV 1 Peter 4:6: “the gospel preached also to them that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) 1 Peter 4:6: νεκροῖς εὐηγγελίσθη … κατὰ ἀνθρώπους σαρκὶ … κατὰ θεὸν πνεύματι [to the dead it was proclaimed … according to men in flesh … according to God in spirit]; the Textus Receptus text served prints the same words. KJV 1 Peter 4:5: “ready to judge the quick and the dead”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/60/4/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/60/4/.
reasoning: The verse states that the gospel was preached to “the dead” and gives a purpose in two halves. It does not say whether the persons were dead at the time of the preaching (the Greek has no verb “were” before “dead”) or became dead afterwards, whether “dead” means physically dead or dead in another sense, or what “according to men in the flesh” and “according to God in the spirit” describe. The verse before it speaks of “the quick and the dead” in the Lord’s judging, and the verse does not say that the dead of 4:6 are the dead of 4:5. Readings that have been held include believers who heard the gospel while living and have since died, those dead in sin, and persons preached to after death. The verses quoted state none of these and the record does not choose among them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to 1 Peter 4:5–6. A word search of the packaged KJV finds “preached also” only at 1 Peter 4:6. The record does not say which reading is right and does not claim that no other passage of the Bible says more. title: Which is “a sin unto death”, and what is meant by death (1 John 5:16–17)?
summary: 1 John 5:16 distinguishes “a sin which is not unto death” from “a sin unto death”, and says of the second “I do not say that he shall pray for it”. The verses do not say what the sin unto death is, whether the death is bodily or of another kind, or whether “I do not say” forbids prayer or only declines to command it.
text: KJV 1 John 5:16: “If any man see his brother sin a sin which is not unto death, he shall ask, and he shall give him life for them that sin not unto death. There is a sin unto death: I do not say that he shall pray for it”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) 1 John 5:16: ἔστιν ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον· οὐ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω ἵνα ἐρωτήσῃ [there is a sin toward death; I do not say that he should ask concerning that one]; the Textus Receptus text served prints the same words. KJV 1 John 5:17: “All unrighteousness is sin: and there is a sin not unto death”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/62/5/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/62/5/.
reasoning: The verses name two kinds of sin by their end (“unto death” and “not unto death”) and say that a man may ask and life be given for one kind. They do not name the sin unto death, say whether the death is the death of the body, of the person’s standing, or another death, or say whether the brother who sins is a believer. They do not say what “I do not say that he shall pray for it” rules out: it declines to say that he shall pray; it does not in terms forbid prayer. Readings that have been held include a particular act of apostasy, a persistent refusal of the faith, and a sin for which the Law prescribed death. The verses quoted state none of these and the record does not choose among them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to 1 John 5:16–17. A word search of the packaged KJV finds “sin unto death” only at Romans 6:16 and 1 John 5:16, and Romans 6:16 does not speak of a kind of sin set against another; the record does not rest on it. The record does not say which reading is right and does not claim that no other passage of the Bible says more.
